title: The dogs fawn on Telemachus
greek: Τηλέμαχον δὲ περίσσαινον κύνες ὑλακόμωροι, οὐδ' ὕλαον προσιόντα (perissainon kunes hulakomōroi, oud' hulaon)
short: The fierce farm dogs, which nearly attacked the beggar, welcome Telemachus silently; Odysseus deduces that a friend is coming.
body: The scene answers the dogs' attack on Odysseus in 14.29-36: the same 'baying' (hulakomōroi) dogs now fawn without barking, and Odysseus, hearing footsteps and seeing them wag, tells Eumaeus that someone they know is approaching. Monro notes that the poet slides from 'he noticed the dogs fawning' to an independent clause for the sound of feet, a slight anacoluthon, and that the dogs' behaviour shows the sympathy with animals so noticeable in the Odyssey (compare 16.162-3 and the old dog Argos at 17.291-327). The motif of dogs recognising those who belong to the house prepares for Argos, who will recognise Odysseus through his disguise when no human can.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 16.6 and 16.162-163.
Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. ὑλακόμωρος.
Homer, Odyssey 17.291-327 (Argos).

title: Simile of the father greeting a returning son
greek: ὡς δὲ πατὴρ ὃν παῖδα φίλα φρονέων ἀγαπάζῃ ἐλθόντ' ἐξ ἀπίης γαίης δεκάτῳ ἐνιαυτῷ, μοῦνον τηλύγετον
short: Eumaeus welcomes Telemachus like a father welcoming an only son home after ten years, while the real father sits watching.
body: This is one of the Odyssey's most poignant 'reverse' similes. Eumaeus, a slave, is compared to a father, and Telemachus to a beloved only son returning in the tenth year from a distant land, a description that fits Odysseus far better than Telemachus, who has been away about a month. Meanwhile the true father, unrecognised, watches the scene. Monro explains apiē gaia as 'a far-off land' and accepts Buttmann's view that tēlugetos means 'beloved, favourite'; LSJ calls its origin uncertain but notes that it is used of a darling or only son. Monro's Appendix uses the following phrase 'as one escaped from death' (16.21) as evidence that the journey to Pylos and Sparta (the Telemachy) was part of the original Odyssey. The simile anticipates the real reunion of father and son later in the book.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 16.18 and 16.19.
D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), Appendix I, p. 317 (on 16.21).
Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. τηλύγετος.

title: 'Sweet light'
greek: ἦλθες, Τηλέμαχε, γλυκερὸν φάος (ēlthes, Tēlemache, glukeron phaos)
short: Eumaeus greets Telemachus as glukeron phaos, 'sweet light', a phrase Penelope repeats when she sees her son.
body: Murray, like most translators, takes 'sweet light' as an affectionate vocative ('light of my eyes'), comparable to Latin mea lux. In his Additional Notes, Monro reports T. L. Agar's argument that in Homer phaos used metaphorically always means 'deliverance' or 'salvation': compare Il. 18.102, where Achilles laments that he did not become 'a light' (a saving help) to Patroclus, and Il. 17.615. On that view the line means 'you have come, Telemachus, as a deliverance', with phaos a predicate rather than a term of endearment; Monro thinks it probably a nominative. Either way, the same words are spoken by Penelope when Telemachus reaches the palace (17.41), so the slave and the mother greet the son identically, another sign of Eumaeus' place almost within the family.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), Additional Notes, on 16.23 (citing T. L. Agar, Journal of Philology 27).
Homer, Iliad 18.102 ('I did not become a light to Patroclus').
Homer, Odyssey 17.41 (Penelope's greeting).

title: Atta: 'father' as affectionate address
greek: ἔσσεται οὕτως, ἄττα (essetai houtōs, atta)
short: Telemachus calls Eumaeus atta, a familiar word for 'father' or 'old man' used to elders.
body: LSJ defines atta as 'a salutation used to elders, father', derived from child-language, and cites Achilles' address to his old tutor Phoenix, atta geraie, 'old father' (Il. 9.607), as well as this line. It is affectionate rather than formal, close to English 'dad' or 'uncle'. Telemachus uses it three times to Eumaeus in this book (16.31, 57, 130). The word reinforces the father-son simile of 16.17-21 and the paradox of the scene: the young master addresses a slave as 'father' while his real father sits in the hut as a stranger. Eumaeus for his part calls Telemachus 'dear child' (teknon, 16.25, 61). The Phoenix parallel is apt, since Phoenix, like Eumaeus, was an exile taken into a royal household who helped raise the hero's son.

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. ἄττα.
Homer, Iliad 9.607 (Achilles to Phoenix).
Homer, Odyssey 16.57 (atta repeated).

title: Odysseus' bed covered with cobwebs
greek: Ὀδυσσῆος δέ που εὐνὴ χήτει ἐνευναίων κάκ' ἀράχνια κεῖται ἔχουσα (chētei eneunaiōn kak' arachnia keitai echousa)
short: Telemachus asks whether his mother has remarried and left Odysseus' bed empty and covered with spider-webs.
body: The image of the unused bed covered with cobwebs expresses abandonment. The cobwebs suit a household whose master is absent. Monro notes that eneunaia may mean either 'sleepers in the bed' or 'bed-coverings', and prefers the latter. He also explains why Telemachus should ask, after only a month away, whether his mother has remarried: the question reminds us that the crisis in Penelope's fortunes is close, and Odysseus has returned only just in time. The marriage bed will become the decisive token of recognition between Odysseus and Penelope in Book 23 (23.177-204), so the cobwebbed bed here is a quiet anticipation of the poem's climax.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 16.33-35 and 16.35.
Homer, Odyssey 23.177-204 (the test of the bed).

anchor: run in but a single line
title: A line of only sons
greek: ὧδε γὰρ ἡμετέρην γενεὴν μούνωσε Κρονίων· μοῦνον Λαέρτην Ἀρκείσιος υἱὸν ἔτικτε (mounōse ... mounon)
short: Telemachus explains that his family has had only one son in each generation: Arceisius, Laertes, Odysseus, himself.
body: The beggar has asked whether Telemachus has no brothers to help him fight, 'in whose fighting a man trusts' (16.97-8; Monro: brothers who do not stand by you as they ought). The reply traces the genealogy: Zeus has 'made single' (mounōse) the family, so that Arceisius had one son, Laertes, who had one son, Odysseus, who had one son. The fourfold repetition of mounon ('only') stresses the house's vulnerability: there are no kinsmen to defend its property, which is why the suitors can devour it. Arceisius, Laertes' father, is named elsewhere (4.755, 14.182, 24.270); later writers gave him various parents, but Homer says nothing of them. The single line also explains why Odysseus' survival matters so much: if Telemachus dies, the house ends.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 16.97.
Homer, Odyssey 16.117-121.
Homer, Odyssey 14.180-182 (Eumaeus fears for the race of Arceisius).

anchor: appear in manifest presence to all
title: Gods visible only to some
greek: οὐ γάρ πω πάντεσσι θεοὶ φαίνονται ἐναργεῖς (ou gar pō pantessi theoi phainontai enargeis)
short: Athena appears as a woman at the door; Odysseus and the dogs see her, Telemachus does not.
body: Enargeis means 'visible, palpable, in bodily shape' (LSJ), and LSJ quotes this line together with Il. 20.131, 'gods are hard to look on when they appear in their own forms'. Homer often lets a god be seen by one person only, as when Athena appears to Achilles alone in the quarrel of Iliad 1 (1.197-8); the Phaeacians, by contrast, say the gods visit them openly (Od. 7.201-3). The dogs see Athena too, and instead of barking slink away whimpering (knuzēthmōi) to the far side of the farm; Monro cites this as another instance of the Odyssey's sympathy with dogs. Athena summons Odysseus with a nod of her brows, tells him to reveal himself to his son, and touches him with her golden wand.

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. ἐναργής.
Homer, Iliad 1.197-198 (Athena seen by Achilles alone).
D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 16.162-163.

title: Odysseus restored, and the colour of his hair
greek: κυάνεαι δ' ἐγένοντο γενειάδες ἀμφὶ γένειον (kuaneai d' egenonto geneiades amphi geneion)
short: Athena gives Odysseus back his youth, colour and clothes; his beard grows 'dark', though his hair was called fair in Book 13.
body: With a touch of her golden wand Athena clothes Odysseus in a clean cloak and tunic, increases his stature and youthful bloom, darkens his complexion, fills out his cheeks and makes his beard kuaneai, 'dark'. Monro points out that this contradicts Book 13, where the hair Athena destroys is xanthai, 'fair, yellow' (13.399, 431). He compares the first edition of Walter Scott's Heart of Midlothian, in which Effie Deans is first black-haired, then brown-haired, then fair, an inconsistency corrected only in later editions; such slips, he suggests, are natural in long narratives before the age of revision. Two manuscripts read etheirades, 'hair', instead of geneiades, 'beard'. Others try to reconcile the two passages by taking xanthos as 'light brown' or kuaneos loosely, but the simplest view is Monro's: the poet's attention is on the transformation, not on consistent colouring.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 16.175 and 16.176, with critical note.
Homer, Odyssey 13.429-431 (fair hair destroyed).
Homer, Odyssey 16.172-176.

anchor: Be sure I am no god
title: 'I am your father': recognition of father and son
greek: οὔ τίς τοι θεός εἰμι· τί μ' ἀθανάτοισιν ἐΐσκεις; ἀλλὰ πατὴρ τεός εἰμι (ou tis toi theos eimi ... alla patēr teos eimi)
short: Telemachus takes the transformed stranger for a god; Odysseus reveals that he is his father, the first recognition of the homecoming.
body: Telemachus, seeing the beggar transformed, turns his eyes away in fear and offers sacrifice, assuming that he faces a god. Odysseus' reply is simple and solemn: 'I am no god ... I am your father.' The words recall Telemachus' own uncertainty in Book 1, when he told the disguised Athena that his mother said he was Odysseus' son, 'but I do not know; no one knows his own father' (1.215-16). Telemachus at first refuses to believe, insisting that only a god could change a man from old to young; Odysseus explains that it is the work of Athena. Odysseus now lets fall the tears he had held back throughout (Monro on 16.191: 'though up to that time he had borne up firmly'), and Monro explains the plural biai at 16.189 as 'the forceful deeds' of the suitors. This is the first of a series of recognitions (Argos, Eurycleia, Penelope, Laertes) that structure the second half of the poem.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 16.189 and 16.191.
Homer, Odyssey 1.215-216 (Telemachus doubts his parentage).
Homer, Odyssey 16.177-212.

title: The twentieth year
greek: ἤλυθον εἰκοστῷ ἔτεϊ ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν (ēluthon eikostōi eteï es patrida gaian)
short: Odysseus' absence has lasted twenty years: ten at Troy and ten in wandering.
body: 'I have come in the twentieth year to my native land' is a line Odysseus will repeat, and the number recurs throughout the second half of the poem: Halitherses had prophesied his return 'in the twentieth year' (2.175), Argos dies having seen him again 'in the twentieth year' (17.327), and Penelope, the nurse and the narrator use the same reckoning (19.484, 21.208, 23.102, 23.170, 24.322). The twenty years divide into ten of war and ten of wandering, seven of them with Calypso. Monro's critical note records that all manuscripts have eikostōi here, but that traces of an older form with the initial digamma (weikostos) justify restoring it; the line is a small example of how editors try to recover earlier pronunciation behind the transmitted text. The emphasis on time measures what Penelope and Telemachus have endured.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), critical note on 16.206.
Homer, Odyssey 2.174-176 (Halitherses' prophecy).
Homer, Odyssey 17.326-327 (Argos).

title: Simile of the birds robbed of their young
greek: κλαῖον δὲ λιγέως, ἀδινώτερον ἤ τ' οἰωνοί, φῆναι ἢ αἰγυπιοὶ γαμψώνυχες (adinōteron ē t' oiōnoi, phēnai ē aigupioi)
short: Father and son weep together louder than sea-eagles or vultures whose nestlings farmers have taken.
body: The simile is a reversal of the situation it describes: the birds cry because they have lost their young, while Odysseus and Telemachus weep because they have found each other. Grief and joy share a single sound, and the image also recalls everything the twenty years have cost. Monro discusses adinōteron, which he connects with adinos 'thick, close-packed', applied to a cry that comes fast and continuous; the comparative may express not a degree but simply the quality, like melanteron 'dark as pitch' at Il. 4.277. Aeschylus uses a similar image at the opening of the Agamemnon, where the sons of Atreus, robbed of Helen, cry out for war like vultures circling over their plundered nest (Agamemnon 49-54). The reunion is so long that the sun would have set on their weeping, says the poet, had Telemachus not asked a practical question.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 16.216.
Aeschylus, Agamemnon 49-54 (the vultures robbed of their young).
Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. ἀδινός.

title: The catalogue of the suitors
greek: ἐκ μὲν Δουλιχίοιο δύω καὶ πεντήκοντα κοῦροι κεκριμένοι (ek men Doulichioio duō kai pentēkonta kouroi kekrimenoi)
short: Telemachus counts the suitors: 52 from Dulichium, 24 from Same, 20 from Zacynthus and 12 from Ithaca, 108 in all, with attendants.
body: The suitors number 108, with six servants for the Dulichians, the herald Medon, the singer (Phemius) and two carvers. Telemachus despairs of two men fighting so many. The catalogue confirms that the suitors are the leading young men of all four islands of Odysseus' kingdom, as Telemachus told Athena in Book 1 (1.245-8). Monro points out a tension: elsewhere the suitors come to the palace each day and go home at night 'each to his own house' in the town (1.424), which is hard to square with men from other islands. He explains it as the kind of unevenness found in long fiction, perhaps eased by the dependent islands' chiefs having lodgings in the capital, rather than a sign of different authors. The large number makes the coming victory with only four fighters, aided by Athena, a matter of divine help as well as cunning.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 16.245 and 16.247-251.
Homer, Odyssey 1.245-248 (the islands of the suitors).
Homer, Odyssey 1.424 (the suitors go home at night).

title: Athena and Zeus as allies
greek: ἐσθλώ τοι τούτω γ' ἐπαμύντορε, τοὺς ἀγορεύεις, ὕψι περ ἐν νεφέεσσι καθημένω (esthlō toi toutō g' epamuntore)
short: Odysseus names Athena and Zeus as his helpers; Telemachus answers drily that they sit very high in the clouds.
body: Monro thinks the point of this exchange is usually missed. When Odysseus asks whether Athena and Father Zeus will be enough, Telemachus answers ironically: excellent champions, no doubt, but they sit far off in the clouds, instead of fighting beside us. Hence Odysseus' firm reply that 'not long' will those two hold aloof from the battle when the might of Ares is tested in his halls. Monro draws attention to the change from toutō ge, 'those two, forsooth', to keinō ge in the answer. The exchange marks Telemachus' growth: he speaks to his father with a young man's frankness and a touch of humour, not with mere obedience. The promise is fulfilled in Book 22, where Athena, disguised as Mentor and then as a swallow on the rafter, turns the battle (22.205-40, 297-9).

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 16.263-264.
Homer, Odyssey 16.258-269.
Homer, Odyssey 22.297-299 (Athena's aegis in the slaughter).

title: The plan to remove the weapons from the hall
greek: ἐκ καπνοῦ κατέθηκ', ἐπεὶ οὐκέτι τοῖσιν ἐῴκει (ek kapnou katethēk', epei ouketi toisin eōikei)
short: Odysseus tells Telemachus to hide the weapons hanging in the hall, explaining to the suitors that the smoke has spoiled them.
body: The arms hanging in the megaron are a danger in the coming fight, so Telemachus is to carry them to the store-room and explain that smoke from the hearth has blackened them, and that Zeus has warned him that drunken men might quarrel and wound one another. Monro reports that these eighteen lines were condemned by Zenodotus and Aristarchus, because the plan does not match what actually happens in 19.4-13, where father and son remove the arms together at night, with no nod or signal in the suitors' presence. He also points out that 'when they miss them' (16.287) suits men struck by the absence of something familiar rather than a signal given in front of them, and finds late linguistic forms in 16.290 and 293. Whether the passage is an addition or simply an anticipation imperfectly carried out is still debated.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 16.281-298, 16.283, 16.288 and 16.290.
Homer, Odyssey 19.4-13 (the arms removed).

anchor: does the iron draw a man
title: 'Iron draws a man to it'
greek: αὐτὸς γὰρ ἐφέλκεται ἄνδρα σίδηρος (autos gar ephelketai andra sidēros)
short: A proverb: weapons lying to hand tempt men to use them; here 'iron' simply means weapons.
body: The line sounds like a proverb and is repeated in Book 19. Monro compares Tacitus, Histories 1.80, where the sight of weapons among drunken soldiers 'stirred a desire for them' (et visa inter temulentos arma cupidinem sui movere). The use of sidēros, 'iron', for weapons is notable, because Homeric warriors normally fight with bronze, and the poems generally reflect a Bronze Age heroic world; Monro draws attention to this mention of iron as the ordinary material of arms and discusses it further in his note on 19.13. The proverb fits Odysseus' strategy precisely: by removing the weapons, he leaves the suitors defenceless when he reveals himself.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 16.294 (with reference to the note on 19.13).
Tacitus, Histories 1.80.
Homer, Odyssey 19.11-13 (the proverb repeated).

anchor: learn the temper of the women
title: Testing the household
greek: ἀλλ' οἶοι σύ τ' ἐγώ τε γυναικῶν γνώομεν ἰθύν (alla oioi su t' egō te gunaikōn gnōomen ithun)
short: Odysseus plans to keep his return secret even from Penelope and to test the loyalty of maids and men; Telemachus advises testing only the women.
body: Testing (peira) is a recurring method of the second half of the Odyssey: Odysseus tests Eumaeus (14.459, 15.304), the suitors, Penelope and finally Laertes. Here he insists that no one, not even Penelope, should know he is home, while he and Telemachus discover which servants are loyal. Telemachus, showing independent judgement, argues that testing every herdsman on the farms would waste time while the suitors devour the house, but agrees that they should learn which of the women 'dishonour thee, and who are guiltless'. Monro discusses the form of the word for 'guiltless' (nēleitides), which he derives from alitein, 'to sin'. The result of the test is grim: twelve of the fifty maids are found disloyal and are hanged after the slaughter (22.421-73).

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 16.313 and 16.317.
Homer, Odyssey 22.421-425 (the twelve disloyal maids).
Homer, Odyssey 16.300-320.

title: Antinous proposes to murder Telemachus
greek: ἀλλὰ φθέωμεν ἑλόντες ἐπ' ἀγροῦ νόσφι πόληος ἢ ἐν ὁδῷ (alla phtheōmen helontes ep' agrou nosphi polēos ē en hodōi)
short: After the failed ambush the suitors meet apart, and Antinous urges them to kill Telemachus before he can rouse the people against them.
body: The suitors' private meeting outside the palace (Monro: they 'held a sitting') shows them as a political faction. Antinous fears that Telemachus will call an assembly, expose their attempted murder and turn the people against them, so that they might be driven into exile. He proposes to kill him in the country or on the road and to divide his property, leaving only the house to Penelope and her new husband. Monro notes the litotes of 'they will not praise us' (16.380), meaning they will be outraged. If this plan displeases them, Antinous offers a lawful alternative: let each suitor stop feasting on Odysseus' goods and court Penelope from his own house with gifts. The speech confirms the suitors' guilt in the poem's moral scheme: they are not merely greedy guests but would-be murderers of the heir.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 16.344, 16.375 and 16.380.
Homer, Odyssey 16.364-392.
Homer, Odyssey 4.663-672 (Antinous plans the ambush).

title: Bride-gifts (hedna)
greek: ἐκ μεγάροιο ἕκαστος μνάσθω ἐέδνοισιν διζήμενος (mnasthō eednoisin dizēmenos)
short: The proper way to win Penelope: each suitor should court her from his own house by offering bride-gifts, and she marry the highest bidder.
body: LSJ defines hedna (eedna) as 'bride-price or wedding-gifts', given by the suitor to the bride's family, as distinct from the dowry given with the bride; but in some passages (for example Od. 1.277 and 2.196) the word seems to mean gifts given by the bride's own family, and scholars disagree about how consistent Homeric marriage customs are. Antinous' alternative describes orderly courtship: offers are sent from each suitor's house and Penelope marries 'whoever offers most and comes as her fated lord'. Monro notes that the phrase implies sending hedna, or at least offers of them, from the several houses. The suitors' real offence is that they court her by consuming her husband's property instead. Penelope later shames them into giving gifts (18.274-303), a scene that depends on this custom.

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. ἕδνον.
D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 16.390-392.
Homer, Odyssey 18.274-280 (Penelope asks for gifts).

title: Amphinomus, the decent suitor
greek: Ἀμφίνομος ... Νίσου φαίδιμος υἱός, Ἀρητιάδαο ἄνακτος (Amphinomos ... Nisou phaidimos huios, Arētiadao anaktos)
short: The leader of the Dulichian suitors, who pleases Penelope and argues against murdering Telemachus, yet dies with the rest.
body: Amphinomus, son of Nisus and grandson of Aretias, leads the Dulichian suitors and 'above all the others he pleased Penelope with his words, for he had an understanding heart'. He refuses to kill a man of royal blood without first consulting the will of the gods. His decency makes his fate tragic. In Book 18 Odysseus, moved by his kindness, warns him to leave before the master returns; he goes away troubled, 'yet not even so did he escape his doom, for Athena bound him to be slain by Telemachus' spear' (18.119-57). In the battle he is the first to charge Odysseus and is struck down from behind by Telemachus (22.89-94). Monro mentions him as evidence that the suitors were the chief men of the four islands. Through Amphinomus the poem asks whether a good man can be guilty by association, and answers harshly.

sources.cite: Homer, Odyssey 18.119-157 (Odysseus' warning to Amphinomus).
Homer, Odyssey 22.89-94 (his death).
D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 16.247-251.

title: 'The oracles of great Zeus' (themistes)
greek: εἰ μέν κ' αἰνήσωσι Διὸς μεγάλοιο θέμιστες (ei men k' ainēsōsi Dios megaloio themistes)
short: Amphinomus proposes to consult the gods' will before killing Telemachus; themistes here means divine pronouncements.
body: Themis is 'that which is laid down or established' (LSJ), custom and right; the plural themistes can mean rulings or decrees, and here, as Monro notes, the 'sentences' or oracles that tell what ought to be done. Strabo preserved an ancient variant, tomouroi, a word for the priests of Zeus at Dodona, which Monro thinks was brought into the text by a learned grammarian. In his Appendix he observes that resort to local oracles is distinctive of the Odyssey and that this sense of themistes is shared with the Homeric Hymn to Apollo. Amphinomus' caution is ironic, since the reader knows that the will of Zeus is already set against the suitors; the oracle he proposes to consult is never asked.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 16.403.
D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), Appendix II, p. 336.
Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. θέμις.

anchor: came to this house a fugitive
title: Penelope's rebuke: Eupeithes the suppliant
greek: ἦ οὐκ οἶσθ' ὅτε δεῦρο πατὴρ τεὸς ἵκετο φεύγων, δῆμον ὑποδείσας; (patēr teos hiketo pheugōn)
short: Penelope reminds Antinous that Odysseus once saved his father Eupeithes from an angry people; the son now repays protection with murder.
body: Informed by the herald Medon, Penelope appears in the hall and accuses Antinous of ignoring 'suppliants, for whom Zeus is witness'. Monro argues that the phrase refers not to Telemachus but to the relation between suppliant and protector: Antinous' father Eupeithes once fled to Odysseus' house after joining Taphian pirates in raiding the Thesprotians, allies of Ithaca, and Odysseus restrained the people who wanted to kill him and seize his property. That act created a sacred bond (hosiē) between the families, which Antinous now violates by devouring the house, wooing the wife and plotting to kill the son. The story also prepares for the end of the poem, where Eupeithes leads the suitors' kinsmen against Odysseus and is killed by Laertes (24.422-71, 520-5).

title: Eurymachus' false reassurance
greek: πολλάκι γούνασιν οἷσιν ἐφεσσάμενος κρέας ὀπτὸν ἐν χείρεσσιν ἔθηκεν (pollaki gounasin hoisin ephessamenos kreas opton)
short: Eurymachus swears to protect Telemachus, recalling how Odysseus fed him on his knees as a child, while himself plotting the boy's death.
body: Eurymachus answers Penelope with emphatic promises: no man shall lay hands on Telemachus while he lives, and he would spill the attacker's blood. His proof of affection is that Odysseus often set him on his knees as a child and gave him roast meat and red wine. The picture closely resembles Phoenix's memory in the Iliad of setting the infant Achilles on his knees and feeding him meat and wine (Il. 9.485-91), a scene of tender foster-parenthood. In Eurymachus' mouth it becomes hypocrisy, and the narrator says so plainly: 'thus he spoke to cheer her, but against that son he was himself plotting death' (16.448). Such direct moral comment from the narrator is rare in Homer and makes the suitors' guilt unmistakable. The contrast with Eumaeus, the slave who truly acted as a father to Telemachus, is pointed.

sources.cite: Homer, Iliad 9.485-491 (Phoenix and the infant Achilles).

title: The hill of Hermes
greek: ὅθι θ' Ἕρμαιος λόφος ἐστίν (hothi th' Hermaios lophos estin)
short: A hill above the town of Ithaca named after Hermes, probably for a wayside cairn sacred to the god of roads.
body: LSJ lists Hermaios lophos at this line as 'called after Hermes' and notes that the ancient scholia explained it as equivalent to hermax, a heap of stones or cairn. Travellers in Greece added stones to such heaps at roadsides and boundaries as offerings to Hermes, the god of roads, travellers and luck, and these cairns are often thought to lie behind the later stone pillars called herms. A Hermaion lepas, 'Hermes' rock' on Lemnos, appears in Aeschylus' beacon speech (Agamemnon 283). From this vantage-point Eumaeus sees the suitors' ship returning from the failed ambush, laden with shields and spears, so that Telemachus learns that his enemies are back in Ithaca.

title: 'Double-pointed' spears
greek: ἔγχεσιν ἀμφιγύοισι (enchesin amphiguoisi)
short: An epithet of spears whose meaning is uncertain: double-pointed, two-edged, or flexible.
body: Amphiguos is always an epithet of the spear in Homer. LSJ offers two explanations: 'with a limb at each end, double-pointed' (from guion, 'limb'), or 'bending both ways, elastic' (from guēs, a curved piece of wood). Monro, citing Helbig, notes that it is uncertain whether the word means a spear sharp at both ends or one whose head is sharp on both sides like a two-edged sword. He quotes the archaeologist J. L. Myres in favour of the second: Mycenaean butt-spikes are rare and unlike lance-heads, whereas Mycenaean and Iron Age spearheads are decidedly two-edged, with hollow-ground blades and a tubular mid-rib. Murray's 'double-pointed' follows the older interpretation. Here the spears simply show that the ship Eumaeus saw was the suitors' armed ambush party returning home.

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. ἀμφίγυος.

anchor: the strong and mighty Telemachus smiled
title: Telemachus' secret smile
greek: μείδησεν δ' ἱερὴ ἲς Τηλεμάχοιο ἐς πατέρ' ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ἰδών, ἀλέεινε δ' ὑφορβόν (meidēsen d' hierē is Tēlemachoio)
short: Hearing that the suitors' ship is back, Telemachus smiles at his father and avoids the swineherd's eye: the first shared secret.
body: The phrase rendered 'the strong and mighty Telemachus' is literally 'the sacred strength of Telemachus' (hierē is), a heroic periphrasis like 'the sacred might of Alcinous' (13.20) or 'of Antinous' (18.34), in which a person is named by his power; LSJ explains hieros in such phrases as 'filled with or manifesting divine power'. Here the grand formula frames a small, intimate gesture. Odysseus has been changed back into an old man before Eumaeus' return (16.454-9), so the swineherd still knows nothing, and Telemachus must hide his feelings. The smile shows that the young man is now an accomplice in his father's deception, able to keep a straight face in the presence of a loyal friend. The book ends with the three men sharing an 'equal feast' and the gift of sleep, a peaceful pause before the move to the palace in Book 17.

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. ἱερός.
